content: The third edition of the Integrated Management of Pregnancy and Childbirth: Pregnancy, Childbirth, Postpartum, and Newborn Care – A Guide for Essential Practice has been updated to incorporate recommendations from recently approved WHO guidelines relevant to maternal and perinatal health. This revised guide provides comprehensive, evidence-based norms and standards to enable healthcare providers at the primary care level to deliver high-quality, integrated care during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period, as well as for newborns. It aims to support countries in ensuring that pregnancy, childbirth, and the early postnatal weeks are safe and positive experiences for all women and children. The guide will be periodically updated as new WHO recommendations become available. The guide represents a collaborative effort between WHO, UNFPA, UNICEF, and the World Bank, reflecting a shared understanding of key strategies to reduce maternal and perinatal mortality and morbidity. These organizations work closely to address these critical health issues. The revisions were carried out by a team of experts and reviewed by over 100 individuals and organizations from more than 35 countries, bringing their expertise and experience to the final text. The guide has also been endorsed by the International Confederation of Midwives, the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics, and the International Pediatric Association. The financial support for the preparation and production of the 2006 version was provided by UNFPA, the World Bank, and the governments of Australia, Japan, and the United States. The current version was revised and updated by a team led by Jelka Zupan and Juana Willumsen, with technical direction and supervision by Maurice Bucagu of WHO/MCA. The guide is designed to assist skilled attendants working at the primary level of healthcare, either in facilities or communities, in managing women during pregnancy, childbirth, postpartum, and post-abortion, as well as newborns during their first week of life. It includes recommendations for managing endemic diseases such as malaria, HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and anemia. The guide promotes early detection of complications, timely and appropriate treatment, and referral when necessary, with the ultimate goal of reducing maternal and perinatal mortality and morbidity. The guide is not intended for immediate use but should first be adapted to local needs and resources. It should address the most serious endemic conditions that skilled birth attendants must manage and align with national treatment guidelines and policies. An accompanying adaptation guide is available to help countries develop their own national guides, training materials, and other supporting resources. The guide is organized into six clinical sections: quick check and emergency management, post-abortion care, antenatal care, labor and delivery, postpartum care, and newborn care. Additional sections address HIV prevention and treatment, support for women with special needs, community links, and guidance on drugs, supplies, equipment, and laboratory tests. The principles of good care, outlined at the beginning of the guide, apply to all women, including those with special needs. These principles emphasize the organization of healthcare visits and overall care delivery. The guide also includes advice on managing newborn problems and links to related WHO documents and resources for further reference.
